p: The Manghud belonged to the Urud-Manghud federation of the Mongolian plateau, and ancient sources derive them from the Kiyat Mongols. The Persian historian Rashid-al-Din Hamadani, who chronicled the Mongols, claimed that many old Mongol clans, the Manghud among them, were founded by members of the Borjigin.

Some Manghud warriors supported Genghis Khan, while a body of them resisted his rise to power. As the Mongol Empire expanded, the Manghud were carried westward with many other Mongol tribes. The clan name was also used for Mongol vanguard troops, though sources differ widely on the military units called mangudai.

In the Golden Horde the Manghud supported Nogai, who died in 1299, and formed a horde of their own, semi-independent of the khans at Sarai. After Nogai's death most of their warriors entered the service of Tokhta Khan. Edigu, who lived from 1352 to 1419 and was the son of the noble Kutlukiya, led the eastern begs and by the end of the 14th century dominated the Golden Horde.

The Nogais guarded the northern borders of the Astrakhan and Crimean khanates and by organised raids into the northern steppes prevented Russian and Lithuanian settlement. Many entered the service of the Crimean khan and contributed to the formation of the Crimean Tatars. About 1630 the Kalmyks, migrating from southern Siberia to the lower Volga, drove the Nogais out; they fled to the plains of the northern Caucasus and to the Crimea, and a small part joined the Kazakh Khanate.

Other Manghits had been settled by Genghis Khan around the city of Qarshi, which remained their base under the Khanate of Bukhara. Their power there grew in the early 18th century through the office of ataliq to the khan. After the death of Nader Shah in 1747 the ataliq Muhammad Rahim Bi had the ruling Abu al-Fayz Khan and his young son killed. The family ruled behind the scenes until the 1780s, when the emir Shah Murad declared himself ruler openly. Not being descendants of Genghis Khan, the Manghits took the Islamic title of emir, not khan, and based their legitimacy on Islam.

The last emir, Mohammed Alim Khan, was ousted by the Soviet Red Army in September 1920 and fled to Afghanistan. Whether his dynasty was of Mongol or of plain Uzbek origin is disputed. The Nogai and Karakalpak peoples are counted among the descendants of the Manghud, and Manghits are found among the Tatars of Russia, the Bashkirs and the Kazakhs, as well as among the Khalkha Mongols of Mongolia.

notes: The article is poorly written and inconsistent: the dynasty is dated 1753-1920 in one place and 1785-1920 in another (the description says 'until 1920', so I gave no start date); the Nogai Horde is said to be founded 'in the 14th century' and 'in the 14th-15th centuries'.
The article says Edigu's father Kutlukiya 'managed to unite all of Jochi's lands under his rule' - the clause probably refers to Edigu; left out.
The article's founding date for the clan ('around early-11th and between 11th Centuries') is garbled and left out.

The article says the three Uzbek khanates claimed 'legitimacy in their descent from Genghis Khan' and elsewhere that the Manghits were not his descendants; I kept only the second, which its lead explains.
'had ... killed' renders 'the assassination of the ruling Abu al-Fayz Khan and his young son Abdalmumin by the ataliq Muhammad Rahim Bi'.
